strengths: Novel application of neural solvers to high-speed flows with adaptive time-stepping; addresses an understudied and well-motivated problem
Well-designed two-phase framework with sound technical motivation—correctly identifies why classical CFL cannot be directly applied
Comprehensive ablation studies on neural CFL components and comparison of multiple architectures (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver) with different timestep conditioning strategies
Clear presentation with strong physical motivation and thorough appendices; new datasets are released for community use
Reasonable one-step prediction errors (~0.5-2% relative error) and visualizations demonstrate the model captures shock structures and flow dynamics
weaknesses: Critical absence of computational speedup measurements: despite claiming 'great potential for neural acceleration,' the paper provides zero evidence of wall-clock time improvements or FLOPs analysis compared to classical solvers—central claim remains unsubstantiated

Extremely small and homogeneous test sets: only 9-10 held-out cases per problem from the same distribution as training data; no generalization to different Mach numbers, geometries, or initial conditions

Lack of essential baselines: no comparison to uniform time-stepping neural solvers (claimed to be inferior but undemonstrated), no comparison to classical solvers, and no ablation removing the neural CFL component

Limited scope: restricted to 2D simulations at modest resolution (128×128, 104×104) with low Mach numbers (≤2.97, barely supersonic not hypersonic); unclear if approach scales to practical 3D problems

Significant error accumulation over time: correlation time drops to 19-22% for gas velocity y-component in coal dust (Figure 7), indicating narrow reliability window; limited analysis of why different fields have vastly different performance

Test-time distribution shift addressed but not thoroughly validated: paper doesn't analyze whether neural CFL predicts timesteps systematically different from training, or verify stability of predicted sequences

Dataset and generalization concerns: only 90 training cases per problem is small for deep learning; no justification for Mach number ranges; no analysis of whether predictions respect physical constraints (e.g., density positivity)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap: high-speed flows require adaptive timestepping, yet classical CFL conditions are inapplicable to coarsened neural models
Physically-grounded design incorporating domain knowledge (spatial gradients, max pooling for wave speed, velocity/sound speed features) showing thoughtful engineering
Comprehensive experimental setup with multiple architectures (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, Transolver) and conditioning strategies (layer norm, spatial-spectral, Euler residuals, MoE)
Strong reproducibility with public code/datasets and extensive implementation details across appendices
Clear presentation with well-articulated motivation and methodology
weaknesses: CRITICAL: No speedup analysis or wall-clock time comparisons despite claiming to accelerate high-speed flow computation—the central motivation is unsupported

Evaluation limited to 2 small, simple datasets (circular blast is 2D Sod variant; coal dust is basic multiphase); tiny test sets (10 and 9 cases); no generalization testing to different geometries or physics regimes

Significant long-horizon error growth: coal dust unrolled error ~16-17% (16× degradation from 1-step), raising concerns for practical applicability and suggesting unaddressed error accumulation mechanisms
Missing critical baselines: no comparison with uniform-timestep solvers, other adaptive methods ([72-76]), or ablations showing adaptive timestepping actually helps rather than hurts learning
Unresolved test-time distribution shift: Figure 3 shows visible ∆t prediction errors; no sensitivity analysis of solver robustness to neural CFL mismatch

Limited technical novelty: neural CFL is straightforward regression, all conditioning strategies borrowed from prior work ([54,55,59-62]), all architectures existing—primary contribution is problem formulation only
Inconsistent design choices: CFL features help coal dust but hurt circular blast; no clear justification for architecture decisions; raises generalization concerns
Incomplete evaluation: no shock-preservation metrics despite high-speed flows being shock-dominated; no error analysis by flow feature type; limited failure mode investigation
Extreme temporal coarsening (500×) without analysis of realism or potential artifacts introduced
Variable performance across configurations with unclear practical guidance; MoE uses 3× more memory with unclear cost-benefit justification

strengths: Addresses novel and important problem: first systematic treatment of high-speed flows with adaptive time-stepping using neural solvers
Well-designed two-phase framework elegantly separating timestep prediction (neural CFL) from flow evolution, addressing fundamental mismatch between training and inference regimes
Physics-informed design with spatial gradients, max pooling, and CFL features demonstrating solid domain knowledge
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (U-Net, F-FNO, CNO, Transolver), two diverse datasets (single-phase and multiphase), and multiple metrics
Physically-motivated timestep conditioning strategies inspired by neural ODEs and Mixture of Experts
Strong reproducibility with publicly available code and datasets, detailed hyperparameters and training procedures
Clear presentation with well-articulated motivation and appropriate background on CFD and neural solvers
weaknesses: Critical omission: no wall-clock time comparisons or speedup factors vs. classical solvers, undermining the core claim of 'acceleration' of fluid modeling
Significant error accumulation over long rollouts: unrolled errors reach 5-7% with correlation time proportion degrading to ~60-61%, limiting practical utility
Limited generalization evidence: only 90-100 training cases with 9-10 test cases; no evaluation on unseen parameter regimes, different flow scenarios, or 3D cases
Multiphase results substantially underperform single-phase (coal dust explosion), with volume fraction errors ~18% vs. ~5-6% for other fields, suggesting scalability challenges not addressed
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing comparisons to simpler adaptive approaches, classical schemes on coarse meshes, and related temporal adaptation methods from recent work
Insufficient analysis of timestep prediction failures: when/why does neural CFL fail? No investigation of stability implications or CFL constraint violations
Validation limited to single CFD solver with no experimental data or comparison to alternative numerical methods
Statistical concerns: very small evaluation sets (9-10 cases) despite tight error bars; sensitivity analyses missing for key design choices (noise level 0.01, coarsening factors, loss functions)

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of why adaptive time-stepping is necessary for high-speed flows
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple neural network architectures and three flow scenarios with extensive visualizations
Physically-informed design incorporating domain knowledge into neural CFL model with features motivated by classical CFL condition
Thorough documentation including detailed appendices, training procedures, and extended results with multiple evaluation metrics
Code promised to be publicly available for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: two-phase approaches and neural CFL modeling are relatively straightforward extensions of existing techniques; conditioning strategies largely adapt existing methods
Quantitative improvements are marginal in one-step setting (Table 2) and dramatically degrade in unrolled predictions (~45% error vs ~10% one-step, Tables 10-11), indicating poor scalability
Fundamental design flaw: single global Δt prediction contradicts the inherently local nature of the CFL condition; no justification for two-phase vs. end-to-end learning
Narrow scope limited to three related shock/blast scenarios (all 2D with one 3D case); no generalization study or comparison to recent adaptive neural PDE solvers
Insufficient statistical rigor: only 3 training runs, no significance testing, missing error bars on main figures; hyperparameter choices not justified

Critical performance gap unaddressed: feature importance analysis (Figure 29) shows only u(t) matters, questioning why complex neural CFL is necessary; dramatic unrolled error growth not adequately explained

Missing key comparisons: no computational cost analysis vs. classical solvers, no physics-informed or other adaptive scheme comparisons, unfair oracle comparison (ground truth Δt has unavailable information at training time)
Mass conservation violations (~0.2% relative deviation) mentioned but not discussed for physical validity; long-term stability properties not analyzed

strengths: Well-motivated framework addressing genuine challenge in neural PDE solvers: adaptive time-stepping for high-speed flows with sharp gradients
Thoughtful two-phase architecture design that separates timestep prediction from flow evolution, enabling balanced training objectives
Comprehensive technical exploration with systematic evaluation of multiple neural architectures and conditioning strategies
Thorough experimental validation spanning three high-speed flow scenarios with extensive metrics (correlation time, TKE, mean flow, mass conservation, grid independence)
High-quality presentation with clear writing, logical organization, and informative visualizations including residuals and comparisons
Physically-grounded design drawing from neural ODE theory, mixture of experts, and classical CFL principles
Detailed ablation studies (Section H) demonstrating importance of neural CFL components
Promising runtime analysis showing potential speedups over classical solvers in appropriate scenarios
weaknesses: Limited component-level novelty: framework combines existing techniques (U-Net, CNO, F-FNO, time-conditioned normalization) without fundamental algorithmic innovations
Incomplete baseline comparisons lacking comparison to other adaptive time-stepping methods for neural solvers and limited classical solver validation
Significant generalization limitations: no out-of-distribution evaluation, no transfer between datasets, timestep model specific to trained domain and parameters
Unclear practical advantages: noticeable errors (1-12% for key metrics), and overall computational efficiency vs classical methods for realistic applications not compelling
Scalability concerns with modest resolutions (max ~256×256), no evaluation on high-resolution grids or 3D applications typical in industry
Dataset and solver specificity: models trained to match HyBurn outputs rather than experimental data; generalization to different numerical schemes unclear
Error accumulation in long rollouts: unrolled predictions show errors approaching 45-46%, questioning utility for extended time horizons
Missing theoretical justification: variance reduction intuition is reasonable but lacks rigorous convergence analysis or formal guarantees
Limited failure mode analysis: insufficient discussion of when/why method fails or what physical phenomena cause difficulty
